[h1]A Classic DOOM Review For First-time Players[/h1]

I'll start off by saying that if you already love classic DOOM and you're looking to hear about the quality of the port: it's great. It comes with every official classic DOOM game/expansion that was ever released, it has lots of difficulty/control customization options, and it has built-in mod support. But I'm not here to talk about that.

Instead, this review is for people like myself, who have never played classic DOOM before and were introduced to the series through DOOM 2016/Eternal, or possibly even another shooter of the same nature like ULTRAKILL. If you're coming into this game expecting a similar experience to those games, then you're most likely going to be disappointed. Classic DOOM has a significantly different gameplay philosophy, and it took me far too long to realize that. 

[h2]My Experience[/h2]

I've tried getting into classic DOOM two times prior to this: 

The first time was in early 2020 leading up to the release of DOOM Eternal, where I did a playthrough of both DOOM 1 and DOOM 2. I treated them like straightforward run and gun games; the same way I treated DOOM 2016. I sped through levels, mindlessly shooting whatever was in my way with no regard to how the levels were designed and no attempt to explore them. This led to many frustrating moments where I would run out of ammo completely, and question why ammo was so limited in a fast paced action FPS. I came out of it thinking the games were okay, but struggled to understand why they're so critically acclaimed aside from their massive impact on the genre. 

The second time was in 2023, where I took a completely different approach to my playthrough in 2020. I explored each level as thoroughly as possible, hell bent on getting 100% kills and secrets. This resulted in the opposite issue: I was entering levels with an overabundance of health and ammo. This turned the game into the straightforward run and gun game that I was treating it as in 2020, except the simplicity of the combat made it feel uninteresting and repetitive. None of my exploration felt rewarding because it was unnecessary. I dropped DOOM 1 less than halfway through the game out of boredom, and dismissed classic DOOM as a primitive relic of the past that doesn't hold up compared to modern DOOM and similar releases.

This is no longer the case. Over the past month I've played through DOOM 1, DOOM 2, and The Plutonia Experiment, which has changed my perspective on the series completely. I want to explain what makes classic DOOM fun, because it's not as obvious as you might expect. 

[h2]What Makes Classic DOOM Fun [/h2]

First, I have an important recommendation. If my description of classic DOOM as run and gun games with simple combat doesn't bother you, then you're free to ignore this recommendation and disregard this review. But if you're looking for more than that and you want to experience this game at its best, then I strongly recommend you listen to what I'm about to say: [b]pistol start every level.[/b] If you aren't already familiar, pistol starting means that you'll enter every level the same way that you enter the first level: 100% health, 0% armor, and nothing but a pistol with 50 bullets. When you select your difficulty, if you press tab then you'll be given the option to pistol start all levels. Levels are inherently designed around pistol start and frequently contain weapon pickups. The rest of this review will be written with pistol starting in mind, in which I'll also explain in more detail why I'm recommending it.

Let me get this out of the way: classic DOOM is not an action game in the same way that modern DOOM is. 

Modern DOOM games are full blown action games that encourage you to be hyper aggressive: in both DOOM 2016 and DOOM Eternal, you have several means of regaining resources mid-fight, and it allows you to take on any fight in an extremely head on manner.

Classic DOOM on the other hand feels more like a hybrid of action and survival. Hitscanners capable of shredding your health make up a good portion of the enemies you'll be fighting, and you're going to be gaining health and ammo primarily through pickups scattered around levels. There will be moments where you're too low on health or ammo to be aggressive, and overcoming those moments is where classic DOOM shines.

Oftentimes you'll be in situations where you're running around a level like a madman, searching for a weapon or ammo while avoiding enemies that are actively pursuing you. Nothing beats moments where you're in a situation like that, and you come across a desperately needed shotgun pickup or a box of shells that enables you to properly fight back. This is why pistol starting levels is so important, as not pistol starting (mostly) strips you of these moments. When you're pistol starting each level, finding a weapon pickup feels so much more satisfying, and exploration/hunting for secrets becomes extremely rewarding. As you die during a level (which you likely will during more challenging levels), you'll become more aware of the level layout, and be able to plan your route in a way that lets you rebuild your arsenal more quickly and efficiently. These games have made me do more pre-planning than I think I ever have in a shooter before. 

Creativity is heavily rewarded as well; there's no objectively correct way to approach a level, it's up to you through trial and error to figure out an approach that works for you. You can immediately dart towards a rocket launcher or plasma gun pickup on the other side of the map, strafing around enemies in your way then dealing with them after you grab it, you can pinpoint and save an invincibility powerup then use it to breeze through a difficult fight that you know is coming up, or you can run circles around enemies and get them to accidentally attack each other then start infighting, saving yourself ammo. Tons of possibilities.

Essentially, what I'm saying is that level design is a huge component in what makes classic DOOM fun. While the combat itself is simple, the way levels are designed require a very thoughtful approach, and make for a super unique and engaging experience. Of course this experience varies depending on each level, as some are more well designed than others, but you definitely feel it when you're playing a good level. If you want to aggressively run through levels while shooting everything on sight, then these might not be the right games for you, and that's okay because plenty of other games fill that niche. But if what I've been describing sounds interesting to you, then these games will definitely be worth your time. 

[h2]Additional Points[/h2]

I'd love to talk more about the positives of these games, but I'm running out of space in this review and I'd mostly be repeating stuff you could hear anywhere else. Yes the enemies are phenomenal, yes the arsenal is solid, and yes the music is great (I love the Andrew Hulshult remixes). Not everything is perfect; some levels make it too easy to avoid enemies or bait them out and slowly kill them near cover, the quality of levels can vary dramatically, the berserk powerup is very poorly communicated (seriously, I'd recommend looking up how it works), and there's some occasional frustrating jank due to technical limitations. But even with these issues in mind, the core of what makes classic DOOM fun still stands. 

I think I'll always prefer the more aggressive combat of modern DOOM, or the verticality of Quake, but classic DOOM provides an incredibly unique experience that no other FPS I've played has provided. Dismissing it as primitive and dated is one of the biggest gaming sins that I've ever committed, and I hate that it took me three attempts to get it. But I'm so glad that I finally do.

Step 7: Launch GZDoom.exe.

The classics are classics for a reason. My house was broken into and they stole all of my electronics except my work laptop, which happened to be with me at the time. Because of that I lost access to all of my gaming consoles and my gaming PC. My work laptop is pretty bare bones but this game and other classics have helped fill the void. It's fun, it's challenging if you want it to be, and metal AF. The graphics are, of course, simple compared to modern First Person Shooters but the enemy designs are cool and the sprites hold up. Being charitable I would say they look cool and rugged. Being uncharitable I can at least say that they are charming. 

For people going through the game on their first try I would recommend taking your time in the levels. There's plenty of power-ups and weapons that make the game more fun and discovering secrets feels good. Save often since some secrets will become inaccessible if you perform (or don't perform) certain actions. 

The game supports mouse and keyboard but I find using the mouse to be a bit unpleasant. Moving it forward moves your character forward as well. It took me a while to figure that out while I was trying to balance on a rising pillar while shooting at enemies and kept falling off. Doom guy will turn at the same rate regardless of whether you use a mouse or the arrow keys so I personally prefer using those and shooting with left ctrl. The game doesn't allow you to aim in the z-axis so Doom guy will automatically shoot above or below so long as the enemy is in your line of sights (the middle of your screen). 

I recommend this game to anyone. It's fun, it has historical value, it's aesthetically very cool and it runs well on a potato.

[h1]Can a game from 1993 still be enjoyable in 2019 without nostalgia goggles? The answer is a resounding YES![/h1]

I booted up Doom with low or even negative expectations—just how good can a game from 1993 be, after all? I had never played anything nearly so old. Must be really outdated, primitive and boring, right? Wrong! Turns out my reservations were entirely misplaced as this game positively blew me away. It is technically primitive in a way, yes, but it plays beautifully with what it has, in spite of the technical limitations of 1993. It doesn't feel constrained by those limitations at all. Hell, modernizing its mechanics, altering them in any way at all, would be a detriment if anything. 

I wasn't entirely convinced after the first chapter due to a lack of challenge (on Ultra Violence), but from the second chapter on I was completely hooked. The gameplay manages to feel fresh and engaging despite the game nearing three decades of age. Each shot has some real punch to it—this is of major importance because the entire game consists mostly of blasting demons—and the mechanics feel overall perfectly tuned. The gameplay is fast, frantic, and wholly satisfying. Doom keeps throwing new toys for you to play with at a steady pace throughout the campaign which all have their strengths. The shotgun is probably the best general-use weapon, but all of the weapons tend to have a niche they excel at—though the shotgun I'd say has a little more long range power than it should. 

Ammunition conservation is also a factor that affects your gun choice as resource management plays a considerable part in Doom. Ammo and other equipment carries over between levels, further increasing the impact of managing your supply. This also lends more value to finding secrets because it's not just the level you find it in that's affected by it; the reward carries far. Secrets sometimes even let you access weapons earlier in the campaigns than they would normally be found. 

The level design is consistently solid, with few if any duds. The game starts off small and forgiving, but as the campaign progresses, the levels get progressively more complex and thronged with ever dangerous enemies. This ensures that the things don't get monotonous as you have to adjust to new enemies and learn their behaviors. Eventually, you'll be fighting multiple enemy types at once and so must know which enemies to prioritize in varying circumstances. It's great fun. 

Most of the game consists in disintegrating droves upon droves of demons, but it also features exploration as a core element. All of the levels are filled with secrets, sometimes even secret levels. More often than not, they're quite cleverly placed. The secrets tend to be quite intuitive and thus hardly feel like a frustrating pixel hunt. They lend the levels significant depth and interest, and perhaps even replay value if you're inclined to find them all. The level designers must be applauded for their efforts on Doom. 

In addition to being revered for its timeless gameplay and marvelous level design, Doom is also known for having a long history with mods and custom maps. There exist multiple source ports, which basically give the game a facelift and make it play more nicely with modern hardware. You *can* play the game out of the box with DOSBox (no pun intended), but I would recommend getting GZDoom. It lets you improve the graphics of the game through options such as high resolutions and texture filtering, and it also lets you change the gameplay by enabling things such as freelook, jump, crouch, and other things. I wouldn't recommend them, however, as I felt that the game is best played as it was originally intended: no freelook, no crouch, no jump. This is a question of preference, though, and some people do prefer having these things on. GZDoom also includes controller support, which I utilized fully as I played through the entire game with an Xbox controller. 

I would recommend downloading a mod called "Beautiful Doom". It improves the graphics in many aspects, including smoothed monster and weapon animations, but doesn't touch the gameplay in any major way—or at all if that's what you choose from its user-friendly settings page. 

I'm pushing my brain hard, trying to think of any flaws to mention about Doom, but I'm at a loss. There's simply little if anything wrong with this game as far as I can think. What it sets out to do it does well, really, really well. One thing that eventually pops into my head is that the boss fights of the game are quite underwhelming. They're easily solved by unloading your guns at the boss, with next to no tactics necessary. They feel more like fighting a strong generic enemy than an engaging and memorable boss fight. Another thing, one that I already briefly mentioned before, is that the shotgun feels a little overpowered at long ranges. It tends to overshadow the chaingun for example. It's nice that the gun feels powerful, but it upsets the weapon balance a little—more so early in the campaign, less in the late. These are minor gripes overall, though. 

All in all, Doom is hands down one of the best shooters I've played in my life. It's a game from 1993 that I played for the first time in 2019, and it didn't feel at all outdated. It really is a timeless classic. If you're at all into FPS games, you should give Doom a go. At 5€/$, there's no excuse not to buy it. Don't be dissuaded by the fact that it's from 1993. I actually prefer this one over DOOM (2016). Turns out the praise Doom receives is not just empty noise from geezers wearing nostalgia glasses.

As I was reading David Kushner's Masters of Doom, I was overcome with a powerful desire to replay DOOM. I grew up with the game. I have fond memories of being eleven or twelve years old and getting my hands on GZDoom for the first time. I had not played video games in a few years, putting a comfortable distance between now and my hardcore days and allowing me to approach a video game with entirely new, sober eyes for the first time in my life.

DOOM might not have been the first first-person shooter but it is the alpha, one of the most important video games to ever exist. It's a watershed moment in history, where the course of gaming was changed forever, elevating it from a silly activity for children into a silly activity for adults. It was equally important to the world of computers, culminating with Bill Gates donning a black trench coat and shotgun in front of a green screen to sell Windows 95 as the Gamer's Operating System. Its impact on the software industry and the 90s as a whole cannot be understated.

Made by a team of only six people, the development of DOOM and the rise of id Software is a picaresque example of the American Dream in action. Programmers, misfits, gamers; highly intelligent, possibly highly autistic too, with a dream and a vision and ludicrous profits from a radical new model of game distribution create something that has never been seen before. It's a classic tale, but does DOOM hold up?

Of course it holds up; in part because of a brilliant decision in tech-anarchism by lead programmer John Carmack in releasing the source code to the public in 1997—allowing fans and programmers to break the game wide open and modify it to their liking, create their own tools, make their own maps, port it to whatever system they wanted and essentially ensuring the game eternal life by doing so—but also because of its stellar design. Where Carmack was the wiz kid, the programmer's programmer and the brains of the operation, Romero was the gamer's gamer and its heart. He knew what made a good level, what monsters needed to be in order to be fun to fight, how they needed to be placed in levels for interesting encounters, and most importantly, he understood the psychology of the player and how to play with their expectations.

It's a masterclass in design. Every monster serves a distinct purpose. They have very distinct attacks. Each monster has a corresponding weapon they are most easily dealt with. The difficulty and fun comes from how these monsters are mixed and matched and where they're placed in the levels. It is so perfect that it approaches quintessence. DOOM is the video game equivalent of chess. This more so applies to the second game, where the roster of monsters was greatly expanded and the addition of the Super Shotgun essentially solved the tediousness that bogs down the latter half of this game.

This brings me to the biggest issue with the first DOOM game: it starts high and ends low. Episode 1 is a blast whereas the other two lose steam quick. Episode 3 is the worst when it should be the coolest because that's when you're actually in hell. The levels get more abstract and less fun to navigate, downright frustrating at points, such as the infamous E3M2 - Slough of Despair, which is essentially a gimmick level, because Sandy Peterson thought it would be cool to make a level shaped like a hand.

But DOOM is more than just the base 3 episodes. Two years later, in 1995, there was an Episode 4, Thy Flesh Consumed. In 2019, John Romero himself returned to make an Episode 5, SIGIL, and in 2023, for the 30th anniversary of the original game, he made SIGIL II. On top of that, there are thousands of brilliant user-made maps that essentially wipe the floor with DOOM's stock levels. There are ridiculous total conversion mods like Batman DOOM. There are mods that are crossovers with other games, like Bloom, mixing the game with 1997’s Blood. Even Bethesda is still keeping it alive with re-releases, ports, and new content.

DOOM is timeless. It might be the one video game that will never be forgotten. Even though I might hate a lot of the later levels. I can always boot up Knee Deep In The Dead for an hour or so of great fun. In an industry where upwards of 85% of all games released before 2010 are no longer commercially available, where games get shutdown a handful of years into their life cycle or downright taken off of download servers for no reason, where current-gen titles get remastered on that same gen lest they become "obscure and forgotten," the persistence and continued cultural relevance of this now over 30 year old game just really warms the heart.
It's Doom. It literally *is* your daddy's computer game, and while it might not visually impress anymore, the actual gameplay is as rock solid now as it was in 1993.

This is it. The classic of classics. While Wolfenstein 3D might have set up the stage, it was DOOM that made the genre one of the staples of PC gaming. Not for nothing were early FPS games called "Doom clones", it was thanks to this game that they become so popular.

First of, I'd like to start with a few words regarding my feelings towards this game, which feels special to me. While Half-Life is my favourite FPS game of all time (and the first one I finished), it was DOOM the first FPS game I ever played. I still remember those computing lessons at the age of four, when my teacher would let me play some DOOM after finishing my tasks. I never got too far, but I enjoyed moving through the levels shooting at stuff. After those lessons stopped, many years went by; I got my own PC and my own games, but I could never get a copy of DOOM, until last week, where I finally thought to myself [i]"hey, maybe I should buy DOOM and try to finish it"[/i], and that's what I did. And I'm glad I did, the game still holds up extremely well.

As I tend to do in all my reviews, I'd like to talk about different aspects: gameplay, story and soundtrack. However, I feel its almost kinda pointless to talk about this game's story, anyone familiar with gaming must have heard of DOOM at least once. In it, you play as a nameless protagonist, the "Doomguy", a space marine stationed in Mars, who must face against the hordes of Hell. Being an early FPS game, there wasn't much more to the story, but it wasn't needed. All we needed were demons to shoot that, and DOOM provided plenty.

The gameplay is pretty much the standard of an FPS game: move through the levels shooting at anything that stands in your path, although a couple of times you also need to find keys to open certain doors. Despite being an old game, the guns feel pretty powerful; firing the shotgun was one of the most pleasant gameplay moments I've found in a shooter, and let's not forget the BFG; there's nothing like shooting a powerful energy beam to obliterate your enemies.

The level design is pretty good, with some relatively large levels for the era, that, in some cases almost feel like mazes (although they aren't frustrating to navigate). And the enemy design is pretty good, offering a nice variety from regular soldiers to things like the Cyberdemon. Finally, the soundtrack is simply amazing.

I can't recommend this game enough. It is, simply put, a classic.

Fast. Brutal. Violent. And with a theme dark enough to match. Grab a gun and blast your way out of the Martian environments now crawling with hordes upon hordes of demons before they drag you down to hell. [h2] DOOM [/h2]

I went into DOOM expecting a game that would feel incredibly dated and that wouldn’t hold up all too well in the modern day, but I was pleasantly surprised. The only parts of DOOM that made it feel old were its simple level design and lack of the ability to look up and down, which hurts aiming a bit.

[h2] DOOM II [/h2]

DOOM II has the addition of new enemies and the glorious Super Shotgun, but is otherwise very similar to DOOM. It shares the same artstyle and has most of the same weapons, but the new features let it differ from DOOM and feel like a new experience. It was a very enjoyable game, but there were a few levels that were confusing and I got very lost and had to watch a walkthrough in order to figure out where I needed to go and what I needed to do. 

[h2] Master Levels for DOOM II [/h2]

This is by far among my least favorite of the games included in this collection and is one of the few games in general I got little to no enjoyment from. Master Levels for DOOM II is just DOOM II but with some of the most frustrating level designs known to man. It was all total nonsense and I have no idea how anybody was supposed to navigate the game normally. One example that still stands out to me was having to walk along a thin, invisible pathway along a wall to access a small room that contained the red key. The only indicator was a barely noticeable detail in the map. There were only a handful of levels where I didn’t need to look up a guide or watch a video. This game alone almost made me not recommend DOOM + DOOM II and I never want to return to it.

[h2] TNT: Evilution [/h2]

TNT: Evilution is when the level design started getting really good. The levels started having more and more small details that make it feel like an actual place instead of a basic environment with a general theme. The game was much more enjoyable and easier to navigate, unlike Master Levels for DOOM II. However, it started to drag and get boring as it went on. Aside from the level design, the game feels very similar to DOOM II and got repetitive, something that persisted through the following games.

[h2] The Plutonia Experiment [/h2]

God is not as forgiving as I once thought.

[h2] No Rest For The Living [/h2]

This one is a breath of fresh air after the previous games. No Rest For The Living still does feel like DOOM II, but is a lot more bearable because it has even more detailed levels than the previous games and doesn’t have absolutely absurd enemy spam like The Plutonia Experiment. It's also really short, which makes it a lot more digestible.

[h2] Sigil [/h2]

While No Rest For The Living is a breath of fresh air, Sigil is completely refreshing. Sigil only uses weapons and enemies from the original DOOM, which not only makes it feel different from the other games, it also makes it so you don’t have to worry about Chaingunners and Revenants. It also has some of my favorite level designs of all of the games included in this collection. I really enjoy having to shoot the hidden eyes in order to progress, and they’re never too difficult to find. It kind of gives it a sense of identity and stands out a little more compared to the other games.

[h2] Sigil II [/h2]

Sigil II is very similar to Sigil, but has a higher difficulty. It handles the difficulty increase better than previous games do. Instead of having insanely complex levels or an absurd number of enemies, it gives you more digestible encounters that are fair and more of a challenge and makes you mindful of your ammo, something you didn’t really have to think about in the other games. The only issue I have with Sigil II is that it gives you a lot of enemies that require a lot of ammo to defeat, or at least a significant amount, like Cacodemons and Barons of Hell.

[h2] Legacy of Rust [/h2]

Legacy of Rust brings back an issue I had with most of the other games. It is difficult, but in an annoying way that feels unfair rather than a reasonable and enjoyable way. It is rather upsetting considering how close this was to being likely the best in this collection. The new weapons and enemies made it feel new and not repetitive, it had unique levels which had new art, the music was phenomenal. Most levels were extremely enjoyable until you reached a certain part that was so annoying that it ruined the entire level. Soul Silo would have become my favorite DOOM level if it weren’t for the [spoiler] eight Cyberdemons [/spoiler] at the end of the level. I ran out of ammo after only killing half of them. I tried running around and getting them to shoot each other for 10 minutes but not one died. It was so close to being super enjoyable but just ended up being really frustrating.

One simple word, one simple game, the absolute best FPS on the planet: DOOM

Straight out of 1993, Doom was a game made simply because the group of 20 something year olds wanted to make it. It's a game where design splashes with creativity, something you don't find in almost any modern game today. 

The game is simple. Get to the end of each stage. That's it. You also need to kill the literal thousands of demon hellspawn along the way so don't forget about them either. The monsters range from simple zombie soldiers to demonic goats that shoot rockets at you. The games monsters all revolve around the notion of avoiding projectiles, or hitscans. 

The maps are designed with absolute love and attention. Each episode was made usually by one person, and you really can feel that distinction when you play them. Some maps were mazes, some maps were huge arenas, some maps used more of a certain ammo type, thus limiting your approach, but most of all, the designs of the maps are interesting and fun to play.

Doom is a testament to the 90's, and a bit to the 80's. The loud metal induced music, the overall design, the action and horror of films such as Aliens. Everything is combined in such a perfect, uniform way that nothing feels out of place.

Doom is in a nutshell, just a game that feels right to play. Not a single aspect about the game feels wrong at all, and that's something you never see anymore in games. The attention to detail and gameplay is absolutely amazing.

There is not one single game I've ever played that did everything as perfect as Doom did. The monsters, the maps, the design, the gameplay, the mechanics, the feel, is all so perfect, that you really need this in your library.

Doom is a game I will always see myself coming back to, even when we are in 2047 playing games on a display device in our brains.

Informational review regarding versions, controls and engines.

This product was previously sold as the "Ultimate Doom" version of the game, which came out in 1995 and featured the original Doom (1993) and the expansion pack: "Episode IV: Thy Flesh Consumed" for MS-DOS. It was emulated with DOSBox here on steam.

In 2019, for Doom's 25th anniversary, id Software released an updated version of the game running on the Unity engine which was ported to the 8th generation consoles. This update, called Doom Enhanced, was later released here on steam as a free update to previous owners of Ultimate Doom, they also changed the store name to DOOM (1993). Fortunately, the original emulated DOS version still comes with this one. The same applies to the steam version of Doom II as well. 

This new re-release, marketed as "Enhanced version", was made in a similar way to the community source ports, like GZDOOM or PrBoom+. It had numerous problems when it released but they managed to [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZRIvHF-msJU]fix pretty much all the issues[/url] and is now considered a very good port. It unfortunately isn't as good as the community source ports in regards to mod support. Despite that, if you're just looking to play a very authentic Doom experience with modern QoL features like 60 fps, high resolution and widescreen support, the Enhanced version is probably the best place to start. 

Nerve Software and Bethesda seem to have aimed for a very vanilla and conservative port, something more akin to the original experience. It even renders the game at a 640x400 resolution internally regardless of the selected output resolution, resulting in a very crisp but low-res image and without the downsides of running a resolution non-native to your monitor. This choice obviously makes the image look "worse" but the chunky pixels fit well with the low-res textures and is more authentic to how the graphics were designed to look. It's a matter of preference though and unfortunately there doesn't seem to be an option to change that.

Nevertheless, If you're looking for the actual vanilla game, you can play the DOSBox version by selecting it in the launch options. You can choose either the DOS version with modern WASD controls or classic controls, in which you move with the arrow keys. Speaking of controls, you can also choose to play with keyboard aiming or mouse aiming, which were both a feature even on the original Doom back in 1993. Although many people claim that Doom only had keyboard controls back in the 90s, that isn't true and is a classic case of the Mandela effect. It is true that many people at the time preferred keyboard aiming but the game actually came out with mouse controls from the get go. John Romero even went on to say that Doom was made for mouse input, so was Wolfenstein 3d ([url=https://soulsphere.org/apocrypha/keyboard/ ]source[/url]. 

The original game didn't have vertical aiming however, that's due to a rendering limitation of the engine. Meaning you could only look left and right and not up and down. Back then, calculating perspective was really taxing on performance, so less angles = faster. 

The first FPS that featured unrestricted vertical mouse-look was Bungie's Marathon back in 1994. Although Ultima Underworld (1992) rendered up and down angles, you had to click the edges of the screen to manipulate the camera. Heretic (1994, Doom engine), while giving you the option to look up and down, restricted it to very small angles and you had to control it via keyboard. In 1995, 3D Realm took note of Bungie's breakthrough and added a similar mouse-look control in its Build engine (Duke Nukem 3D 1996). That said, all of these games that let you control the camera vertically one way or another, didn't really re-render the scene like you'd expect and relied on visual trickeries to change the view. They did it by shifting the horizon line up or down instead of changing your perspective, that's so they didn't need to calculate any of the 3-point perspective distortions that we see in the real world. Hence why they all felt unnatural.

These engine limitations were one of the reasons that Quake (1996) was such a big deal when it came out, and why people call earlier FPS titles 2.5D in retrospect. It wasn't until Quake that full 3-point perspective became a norm in the industry, made possible with the arrival of hardware acceleration technologies. Eventually, since the release of Doom engine's source code in 1999, various community source ports were made. Some, such as GZDOOM added hardware-acceleration rendering options like OpenGL and Vulkan, which allowed real up and down perspective rendering like Quake and all modern 3D games.

Here are a couple of useful tips if you're playing in the DOSBox version:

Movement was binded to mouse input, overlapping your movement keys which will feel very strange if you're used to more modern FPS movement controls. You can disable this forward and backward movement with [url=https://www.pcgamingwiki.com/wiki/Doom_(1993)#Disable_vertical_mouse_movement_.28DOS.29]novert[/url]. 

You should also correct the aspect ratio to the original 4:3 otherwise the game will look squashed. That's because, like many games at the time, the original graphics were designed for monitors that [url=https://doom.fandom.com/wiki/Aspect_ratio]vertically stretched the image natively[/url]. I.e. the original 320x200 resolution is a 16:10 logical aspect ratio but ran on monitors with a 4:3 aspect ratio that stretched the image up and down to fit it, and at the time, graphics were designed to account for that. To correct this, just change the following lines on ultimatem.conf and ultimate.conf files in the game folder to: 


[code][sdl]
output=ddraw[/code]

And:

[code][render]
aspect=true[/code]

Both of these issues were already corrected in the Unity source port (Enhanced Version).

[b]The chicken or the egg but what exactly does that have to do with Doom?[/b]

From that point of view, it's actually nothing at all, but with Doom it's often the case that sentences like "... the game that revolutionized computer games" are often used.
And this is exactly where opinions differ as there were other games before and after Doom that have or could have contributed to this so-called “revolution”.
To list them all would go beyond the scope and when it comes to the id Software games, Wolfenstein 3D is often mentioned or argued about which of the two games triggered this revolution.
ID Software, which initially only released side-scrollers and a few puzzle games, celebrated its first shooter debut in April 1991 with Hovertank 3D, followed by Catacomb 3D, which no one really talks about.
[url]https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cquMrfmLkJ0[/url]
[url]https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=F5MzKdjIaPU[/url]
And if you look at the videos, you can quickly see which games developed from what.

And then if we go by further development and the release date, Wolfenstein 3D, which was released in May 1992, would be the revolutionary game and not Doom, which was released in December 1993.
But what is probably the fundamental difference between the two games, and what most people are probably aiming for when they say Doom revolutionized gaming, is probably the point that Doom uses network mode over the IPX protocol, in which up to 4 players can play on the network.
And that in turn helped to boost the entire LAN party scene that existed in every living room or party room at the time.

So I would say that it doesn't really matter which game or games contributed to it, because there were many games at that time that were revolutionary and these revolutionary games still exist today. Perhaps the difference between then and now is simply that at that time and with the technical possibilities, the steps were bigger and more obvious than perhaps is the case at the moment. Or maybe it just felt that way.
And we can be happy and grateful that it all turned out this way. Without all of this we wouldn't be sitting here playing with joy and with friends, so in the end it doesn't matter which game(s) it was.

[b]Doom the First and why it's now called Doom (1993)[/b]

This is simply because Doom got a reboot in 2016 and is therefore also called Doom (2016).
By the way, Doom (2016) is not, as is often said, the fourth part.
It is simply a reboot of the first game and just as Doom 64 (1997) is not the 64th part, but a game developed for the Nintendo 64 by Midway Games in coordination with id Software that takes place after the events of Doom 2 .
Bugthesda then re-released Doom 64 in March 2020, which was developed by Nightdive Studios.
So much for that.

[b]Shoot, shoot and shoot some more[/b]

Doom, like many other id Software games, was distributed as shareware which only contained the episode “Knee Deep in the Death”. The other two parts, “The Shores of Hell” and “Inferno,” were only delivered after registration. And anyone who had a 468 with 33 MHz or higher (no, that's not a typo, it's really 33MHz and not GHz, even if it's hard to imagine for some) could look forward to up to 50 frames per second.

The story about Doom itself is quickly explained, as there isn't actually a real one and in Doom it's pretty irrelevant.
In short, it's about the UAC (Union Aerospace Corporation) which conducts experiments with teleportation and unintentionally opens a portal on the two Martian moons Phobos and Deimos. As it quickly turns out, these were portals to hell and demons occupied the research facility, killing all the employees and turning them into zombies.

We take on the role of the (still) nameless Space Marine who is on the moon Phobos and is armed with nothing but a pistol. The arsenal expands later in the game to include the well-known chainsaw, shotgun, rocket launcher, gatling and plasma gun and the even more fictional BFG 9000, which, according to id Software, goes by the name “Big Fucking Gun”. 
After we have reached Phobos, we teleport from there to the second moon of Mars, Deimos, which is no longer in the orbit of the planet, but in the hell dimension from which all the monsters come.
After we have destroyed all the monsters there, we head straight to hell to search for the origin of the demonic invasion...

[b]The good old gameplay[/b]

The whole game is designed for speed and requires the player to have very good reactions. The opponents often appear unexpectedly from countless corners or wait for us behind closed doors. At first the controls definitely take some getting used to, which is because the controls are very imprecise and the viewing angle is only designed to turn right or left.

Finding the right path is not always that easy because door switches and secret rooms in particular are well hidden. Red, yellow or blue doors also appear again and again in the game and require the right key card. You often have to fight through the same hallways and rooms in search of the key cards you need.

What didn't exist in 1993 was stunning 4k HDR graphics. The pixel graphics can seem a bit intimidating if you are not familiar with them from the past few days, but you quickly get used to them. The destroyed enemies or objects that always turn towards the player on their own axis are sure to provide a little amusement for some people. This is probably because the objects in the 3D rooms were only designed in 2D, which saved time and storage space.

The sound is probably more of a matter of taste. This consists of pure synthesizer sounds and is absolutely cool in some levels and some levels have a terrible sound. The weapon sounds, on the other hand, sound good, but the whole game lacks a few background noises, so it somehow seems a bit empty.

Even though more than 25 years have passed since its release, the game has lost nothing in terms of quality and is good proof that games can age gracefully. It's still a lot of fun today to explore the labyrinth-like environment in which death lurks behind every corner. Doom would certainly be half as exciting without the great weapons because they are pure fun.

Today's version also includes the fourth episode "Thy Flesh Consumed", which was only released in the expanded version "The Ultimate Doom" (1995).

For the 25th anniversary, the game became the enhanced version, which, in addition to improved graphics, mouse and keyboard controls, controller support, was given widescreen support and native 60 FPS. Local split-screen co-op and PvP mode as well as community add-ons are also available when you register in the Slayers Club.

Doom fans and nostalgics will get their money's worth here.
The pixel graphics and controls may initially cause a few problems for newcomers. But once you get used to it, the game is still fun today and it is definitely a game you should play.

DOOM rocks so frickin’ much dude.
Probably one of the most important and influential shooters of all time and despite its age it’s still such a blast to play today.

The movement is simple but so fast and fluid, and just plain fun to control. 
The weapon variety is so well balanced with them all having their own different strengths and use case scenarios and they all just feel so GOOD to use!

- Berserk Punch, turns the level into a game of Punch Out, great for conserving ammo.
- Chainsaw, stunlocks lower tier demons and is good at saving ammo.
- The pistol… okay, sucks but it takes at most 10 seconds to get something better.
- Shotgun: Classic Workhorse, great at taking out low tier demons, even semi-decent for sniping.
- Super Shotgun: Outright one of the best weapons ever coded into a video game. One blast, 20 pellets, perfect for close range drive-bys paired with your mobility. A clean shot does about the same damage as a rocket. Most satisfying weapon to use in a game full of incredible weapons.
- Chaingun: Good single target damage and mows down a group of low tiers. Great at stun locking in a pinch and your best hits can weapon for sniping.
- Rocket Launcher: High Risk, High reward. Fires fast and the AoE makes it incredible at dealing with crowds. Just try not to face-rocket yourself.
- Plasma Gun: High damage, fast firing rate, best used in a pinch, and reliable in any situation if you have the ammo. Shame it shares it with…
The BFG-9000: Rare, but oh so powerful. Nukes everything in front of you. It even eviscerates boss monsters if you know how to use it right.

Topped all of with the monster variety, which is near PERFECT (Doom 2 specifically). So many different monster combinations for unique and varied encounters. Dangerous enough to not be complete push overs so your approach to combat isn’t mindless, and JUST enough health to keep them as threats but never being too spongey to make them tedious.

Doom’s gameplay loop has such an immaculate flow, than just makes it so good to play. I really do think that the only thing that may be a little outdated is some of its level design and even then a lot of base game’s ones are still good and memorable.

The modding scene is so huge, Honestly I could reccomend Doom 10 times over based on that alone.

Even after all this time, there’s something about Doom’s sprite based art style that’s still so timeless. I will admit many of the base game levels aren’t exactly lookers, but given that you’re playing a custom mapset, Doom has so much potential to actually look so visually stunning and distinct from anything else.

Side note: Doom already has a pretty good soundtrack already, but the Doom community is home to some of the most talented MIDI musicians you’ll ever find. I’d reccomend you play through The Plutonia Experiment, the Master Levels and No Rest for the Living using the community midi packs if you can figure out how to setup those up.

My biggest recommendation is if you come out of the main games enjoying the basic combat and gameplay loop, please do check out the modding scene on Doomworld. It’s legitimately so worth the trouble figuring out to configure a custom source port to play so many unforgettable mapsets and experiences.

(Personal recommendations are: Valiant, Speed of Doom, Back to Saturn X Episode 1, Scythe II, Ancient Aliens, Grove and MyHouse.wad just to name a few)

It feels really corny to say, but Classic Doom really is Eternal. There’s a reason there’s still an extremely dedicated and active community for it. It’s already so worth playing it just for its historical value alone, but it also just happens to be just an incredible FPS game today. I couldn’t reccomend it enough.

So what are you waiting for?!  Buy this game, grab that shotgun and blast those demons back to h*ck!
